cases.abstract: VoxPoser grounds language-specified manipulation subtasks in spatial objectives that motion planners can optimize. Instead of asking a language model to parameterize actions directly, it uses generated programs to query visual perception and compose three-dimensional value maps for robot, object, or object-part motion. Planning against these maps and replanning from observations connects language constraints to executable trajectories without additional training in the zero-shot setting. Across five real-world tabletop tasks, success is 88% in static scenes and 70% with disturbances, versus 24% and 0% for an LLM using simple action primitives. On 13 simulated tasks, category averages favor VoxPoser across seen and unseen instruction/attribute splits, but individual tasks sometimes favor baselines. A complementary contribution uses synthesized trajectories as exploration priors for online dynamics learning: on three simulated contact-rich tasks, success rises from 3.3-18.3% zero-shot to 80.0-91.7%, with mean interaction times below three minutes, whereas learning without priors exceeds a 12-hour limit. These results support spatially grounded trajectory synthesis and targeted adaptation, while perception errors, restricted environment dynamics, and end-effector-only planning constrain the demonstrated capabilities.
cases.notes: Central contribution: executable spatial objectives, not LLM task decomposition. Evidence: real-world success and split-level simulation comparisons; Table 4 prevents a claim of per-task dominance. Retained online dynamics learning as a separate co-contribution, explicitly simulator-only and distinct from training-free execution. Contact-rich zero-shot failures and perception/dynamics limitations delimit the claims.

cases.abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) targets generalization by minimizing the worst training loss within a parameter neighborhood instead of optimizing a single point. A PAC-Bayesian bound motivates this objective under assumptions including that Gaussian weight perturbations do not lower population loss. The practical approximation uses one gradient to construct a loss-increasing perturbation and a second, evaluated at perturbed weights, to update the original parameters. On CIFAR models trained from scratch, SAM improves all tested configurations although non-SAM baselines may train for twice as many epochs; WideResNet CIFAR-10 error with AutoAugment decreases from 2.2% to 1.6%. Gains also occur for ImageNet ResNets and EfficientNet finetuning after ImageNet or ImageNet-plus-JFT pretraining. Under random label noise, SAM improves clean-test accuracy over SGD but trails MentorMix without bootstrapping; one augmented SVHN configuration also worsens. Hessian measurements show lower curvature in the tested model. A further contribution defines m-sharpness on data subsets: smaller subsets improve generalization and predict generalization gaps better in the evaluated settings. The evidence supports approximate neighborhood-aware optimization and subset-level sharpness diagnostics, not a generalization guarantee for the implemented optimizer.
cases.notes: Prioritized the optimizer's neighborhood-loss objective and empirical generalization, preserving the conditional bound and m-sharpness diagnostic. CIFAR comparison retains the doubled-epoch baseline allowance; EfficientNet results retain pretraining provenance. Label-noise superiority is restricted to SGD, with MentorMix and the SVHN regression preventing uniform-superiority language. The bound is not transferred to approximate minibatch updates.
